title: The Blue Book Exercise: Only a Human Can Change Its Mind
author: Terry Underwood, PhD
summary: Terry Underwood offers a work of narrative fiction to explore how one composite/imaginary writing teacher is responding to generative AI's incursion into the classroom. The teacher, exhausted from a summer of 'battling AI,' designs a blue-book writing routine as a deliberate, almost defiant counter-measure, treating handwritten, in-class composition as a bulwark for authentic student thinking. Underwood frames the piece explicitly as fiction, but uses it to dramatize a real tension many writing teachers feel: the pull to protect drafting and revision as human, cognitively necessary acts against tools that can produce fluent text instantly. The teacher is portrayed as both sympathetic and self-aware of his own performativity, staging vigilance for effect as much as substance. Underwood closes by extending solidarity to real teachers doing their best under unrealistic pressure, rejecting the idea that ignoring AI is a viable option. The piece functions less as policy prescription and more as a meditation on what is lost and defended when a teacher insists a mind must change on paper, not through a prompt.
points: Uses fiction rather than argument to explore a teacher's emotional and ethical response to AI in the writing classroom.
Frames blue books/in-class handwritten drafting as a deliberate pedagogical defense of authentic thinking, not mere nostalgia.
Portrays the teacher's vigilance as partly genuine, partly theatrical — a performance meant to reset classroom norms.
Positions 'ignoring AI' as an unrealistic option for today's writing teachers, whatever stance they take.
Reads as a defense of the idea that only a human mind can truly revise and change itself through the act of writing.
quotes: As writing teachers return to the classroom after summer break, many are wrestling with how to handle AI.
The following is a work of narrative fiction about one teacher's radical, flawed, deeply felt defense of human thought and language.
I salute every writing teacher actively working to make sense of this new reality by doing the best they can with what they have in their current circumstances. Ignoring it isn't realistic.
It matters not whether he reads the words. Pausing at the rear of the room, displaying curiosity, he is being performative. Everyone knows it or soon will. Everyone will soon expect it.
Blue books are blessed in this classroom. Inky words on paper are valorized in a strange compression of drafting and revision, the two crucial parts of the writer's process, in his humble opinion.
This imaginary writing teacher is convinced AI companies are trying to destroy the writing classroom, wittingly or not.
He sees himself as a guardian of the tower and makes no apologies about it.
He began the past summer totally exhausted from battling AI. He promised himself that he would come up with a way to move against this rapidly growing monstrosity, and he did.
